text: Chapter 4 built a real, reusable Terraform module — a separate .tf configuration with its own inputs and outputs, referenced by source. Bicep has the exact same idea in different syntax. This lesson covers the module keyword, which calls a separate .bicep file as a nested deployment, and the two ways to supply different values per environment: the newer, typed .bicepparam file and the older JSON parameter file format you'll still find in existing repositories.

A Bicep module is just another .bicep file. modules/network.bicep declares param vnetName and param addressPrefix, builds a Microsoft.Network/virtualNetworks resource from them, and exposes output vnetId string = vnet.id for the caller to read. Nothing about that file is special syntax — it's a complete, independently valid Bicep template, the same way a Terraform module is just a .tf configuration with variables and outputs of its own, sitting in its own folder.

The caller uses module network 'modules/network.bicep' = { ... }, passing vnetName and addressPrefix in through params, the same way you'd pass variables into a Terraform module block. network.outputs.vnetId reads the value straight back out. The name: 'networkDeployment' inside that block isn't the virtual network's name at all — it's the name Bicep gives the inner nested deployment it creates for that module call, and it's what shows up in the Azure Portal's deployment history when you go looking for it later.

Chapter 5 covered Terraform variable files per environment — prod.tfvars, dev.tfvars. Bicep's equivalent is a .bicepparam file, tied to one specific template by a using statement at the top, like using 'main.bicep'. Because that tie-in is explicit, Bicep checks a .bicepparam file's values against the template's actual parameter types at compile time, catching a typo'd name or a wrong type before deployment instead of after. The older JSON parameter file format still works and still deploys with the same az deployment group create command, but it isn't checked against the template that way, and new projects should default to .bicepparam instead.

Modules split a deployment into reusable pieces, and parameter files supply the right values per environment, mirroring what Terraform modules and variable files already do. Next lesson: previewing a deployment before it runs, and the newer deployment stacks feature for managing a deployment's full resource lifecycle.
